questions.topic: A neutral's reply about armed merchant shipping
questions.learningObjective: State what a neutral government's reply to a complaint at sea asserted

options.text: That neutral merchant ships might be armed and trade with all parties, and visits needed grounds
That a neutral government must not permit any merchant vessel to carry a gun at all
options.misconception: Believes neutral ships were required to be unarmed

options.text: That neutral merchant ships were liable to seizure whenever a belligerent suspected them
options.misconception: Turns the right of visit into automatic capture

options.text: That neutrals must withdraw from all trade with a belligerent once hostilities began
options.misconception: Makes neutrality a demand for total commercial abstention

questions.explanation: The reply asserted a neutral's right to arm its merchant ships and trade with all parties, and required any visit to rest on grounds the ship could answer. It did not bar the guns.
questions.hint: Armed, trading, and answerable on grounds.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two readings of the argument for entering the war
questions.learningObjective: Explain the two readings of the case for entering the war
questions.stem: The extractor ran hot, and I wrote in the logbook the two readings of the case for entering the war, and what each one claimed the country was owed.

answer.exemplar: One reading held that the war had become a question of right rather than of advantage: small nations had been overrun, neutral rights had been violated, and a country that stood aside would be counted with the aggressors. The other reading held that the argument was about security and trade: a great industrial power across the sea would dominate markets and bully smaller states, and a nation that stayed out would find its commerce closed and its position steadily reduced. The first reading insisted on a moral settlement, the second on a balance of power that would leave the country strong.

questions.explanation: One reading rested on right and on the protection of smaller states; the other on security, trade, and the balance of power. They agreed on entering and disagreed entirely on what the war was for.
questions.hint: Right and protection against security and trade.

options.text: The constitution said nothing about how a contested election should be settled
The constitution named the House of Representatives as the final judge of every dispute
options.misconception: Invents a constitutional role for the House

options.text: The constitution fixed a single day on which the result must be declared
options.misconception: Invents a constitutional deadline for the result

options.text: The constitution provided that the loser should ask the Senate to decide the contest
options.misconception: Turns a settling mechanism into a Senate role

questions.explanation: The constitution was silent on how a contested return should be resolved, and that silence is why the answer had to be built by statute. No house, senate, or fixed day had a constitutional part.
questions.hint: Silence in the text, so statute fills it.

questions.topic: Two readings of combining production with distribution
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an industrialist's pamphlet as a reading of combination

options.text: Coordination, on the ground that control of production and sale would let output be regulated
Compromise, on the ground that combining firms would make cheap goods for the household
options.misconception: Makes combination a device for cheap goods

options.text: Charity, on the ground that the larger concern would pay better than the small shop
options.misconception: Turns a business argument into a claim of benevolence

options.text: Ceremony, on the ground that the older agreements of the trade had already lapsed
options.misconception: Offers no reason at all for combination

questions.explanation: The pamphlet argued from coordination: controlling production and sale allowed output to be regulated and ruinous competition prevented. It appealed to neither cheap goods nor benevolence.

questions.topic: The shorter-hours argument and what it assumed
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumptions behind the argument for shorter hours

stimulus.body: I copied this from the tract in the drawer: eight hours of work will produce as much as ten, and the worker who is freed at the end of the eight will buy what he needs with the wages he has saved.

questions.stem: Supers went on the tall hive, and I read the tract into the logbook and asked what the argument for shorter hours assumed about what the freed worker would do.

options.text: That output would not fall with the hours, and that saved wages would be spent to sustain demand
That output would rise in proportion to the hours saved, and that wages would fall
options.misconception: Invents a mechanical relation between hours and output

options.text: That employers could not shorten the day, so the shorter hours would come by statute alone
options.misconception: Turns the assumption into a legal claim

options.text: That the shorter day would be paid at a lower hourly rate than the longer one
options.misconception: Assumes a cut in the hourly rate

questions.explanation: The argument assumed the same work would be done in fewer hours and that the freed worker would spend his saved wages, holding demand up. It did not assume output would rise as hours fell.
questions.hint: Same work, saved wages, spending follows.

questions.stem: Propolis sealed a crack in the roof, and I wrote in the logbook that when a returned election was contested, the constitution gave no answer, and I asked what filled the gap.

options.misconception: Invents a single ruling that settled the counting

options.misconception: Imports a parliamentary practice into the constitution

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission on industrial organisation
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a commission on industrial organisation was set up to discover
questions.stem: Feeding syrup went on at dusk, and I wrote out in the logbook what a commission of inquiry into industrial organisation was set up to discover, and what it reported.

answer.exemplar: The commission was appointed because the country's industries had been reorganised into large units and no one could say how far the control of those units had reached. It gathered the corporate records, examined the boards of directors of the largest companies, took the testimony of employers, organisers, and public men, and reported on the concentration of control in particular trades. Its answer was descriptive and alarming: interlocking directorates let the same men direct competing companies, and the law then had no effective answer to that arrangement.

questions.explanation: The commission was appointed to measure how far control had concentrated in the large industries, and it reported on interlocking directorates and the weakness of the existing law. It described rather than dissolved.
questions.hint: It measured concentration, then reported.

options.misconception: Puts the attack on the middleman before the efficiency claim

options.misconception: Puts price steadiness before the efficiency claim

options.text: He closed by appealing to the public interest in cheap and plentiful goods
options.misconception: Puts the appeal to the public first

questions.explanation: The efficiency claim came first, since the rest rested on it, and the attack on the middleman followed from it. A steady price was a result of control, not the starting point.
questions.hint: Begin with the claim about output and waste.

questions.topic: The shorter-hours argument and what it assumed
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumptions on which the shorter-hours argument rested

stimulus.body: I copied this from the printer's sheet: the shortening of the day's labour will not reduce the quantity of work done, for the worker will make up in diligence what he saves in hours, and the demand for goods will rise with the wages he is paid.

questions.stem: The extractor drum was sticky, and I copied the printer's sheet into the logbook and set out the two assumptions the shorter-hours argument relied on.

options.text: That output would not fall with the hours, and that the added leisure would be spent on goods
That employers would refuse the shorter day unless the law compelled them to accept it
options.misconception: Turns an assumption about output into a legal claim

options.text: That wages must fall in proportion to the hours worked, so that output held steady
options.misconception: Assumes a proportional fall in wages

options.text: That the shorter day would be introduced first in the trades least affected by competition
options.misconception: Invents a trade ordering for reform

questions.explanation: The argument assumed the same output in fewer hours, and that the freed worker would spend his earnings so demand would hold. Neither falling wages nor a compulsory statute was part of it.

questions.topic: From a price agreement to a single corporation
questions.learningObjective: Identify what was needed to make a price agreement binding

stimulus.body: I copied this from the trade circular: the refiners of this state will not sell below the figures set out below, and any refiner found selling below them will be excluded from the association and its deliveries.

questions.stem: Migratory yards by the river this season, and I read the trade circular into the logbook and asked what had to change before the agreement could bind anyone.

options.text: A means of enforcing the price, since without a penalty an agreement among sellers held nothing
A royal charter, since the crown alone could make such an agreement enforceable
options.misconception: Invents a charter as the enforcement device

options.text: A written contract, since the law ignored anything not put into writing
options.misconception: Overstates the writing requirement for enforcement

options.text: An act of parliament, since no private agreement could offend the common law
options.misconception: Makes a statute necessary to any binding agreement

questions.explanation: An agreement among sellers bound nobody without a means of enforcing the price, and the circular's penalty was exclusion from deliveries. No charter, writing rule, or statute was needed.
questions.hint: A penalty makes the promise bite.

stimulus.body: I copied this from the printed reply: the undersigned declares that the flag of his state shall not be departed from in the carrying of merchandise in time of war, and that the trade of his subjects shall be open to all nations without exception.

questions.stem: Requeening took the second pair, and I set the printed reply into the logbook and asked what it claimed for the neutral state and its merchants.

options.text: That neutral shipping would carry trade for all belligerents alike, without abandoning either side
That neutral shipping would serve only the side that had not violated neutral rights
options.misconception: Turns neutrality into a partisan alignment

options.text: That neutral merchants would give up the carriage of contraband entirely
options.misconception: Makes neutrality a ban on the contraband trade

options.text: That neutral merchants would carry only for their own flag's commerce
options.misconception: Restricts the trade to domestic cargo

questions.explanation: The reply claimed neutral trade would be open to all nations and that neutrality did not mean choosing a side. The carriage of contraband remained a separate question under the law of the sea.
questions.hint: Open to all, no side chosen.

questions.explanation: The commission studied the general condition of industrial organisation rather than one company, and it did examine the great corporations and the law governing them. Prices were inside its field.
questions.hint: General condition, not a single case.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two readings of combining production with distribution
questions.learningObjective: Explain the two readings of combining production with distribution
questions.stem: Autumn robbing at the weak hive, and I wrote out in the logbook the two readings of combining production with distribution, and who each reading favoured.

answer.exemplar: One reading treated the combination as an economy: a firm that made the goods and sold them itself could coordinate output, remove the duplicate handling and the double margin, and so serve the market at a lower cost. The other reading treated the same arrangement as a danger: a firm controlling the whole chain could shut out competitors from the market it had captured, and the savings would be kept rather than passed on. The first reading favoured the large firm because it was efficient; the second favoured the small firm because it was exposed.

questions.explanation: The efficiency reading favoured the large firm, and the foreclosure reading favoured the small firm that the combined concern could shut out. Both accepted the same arrangement and judged its consequences differently.
questions.hint: One reading favours the giant, one the small shop.

questions.learningObjective: List the claims made on each side of the combination debate

questions.topic: The shorter-hours argument and what it assumed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the eight-hour argument appealed and what it depended on
questions.stem: Winter wrap went on at dusk, and I wrote out in the logbook why the eight-hour argument appealed so strongly, and the condition on which it stood.

answer.exemplar: The appeal was that the whole gain of the shorter day would go to the worker, if the country were willing to accept the argument that the same goods could be produced in fewer hours and that what the worker saved in leisure he would spend to keep the market alive. If a shorter day reduced output, the shorter week would mean less work at the same pay, and employers would resist; if the worker's savings were hoarded rather than spent, the demand that justified the shorter day would weaken. questions.hint: Two assumptions have to hold together.

questions.topic: A neutral's reply about armed merchant shipping
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a neutral answered a complaint at sea with a claim of right
questions.stem: Mites thinned the weak colony, and I explained in the logbook why a neutral government answered a complaint at sea with a claim of right rather than with an apology.

answer.exemplar: A neutral government had two things to defend: the freedom of its flag to carry trade, and the dignity of its law against the claims of a belligerent at sea. Answering with an apology would concede the very visit and seizure that was complained of, and would make the complaint the measure of neutral rights. By stating a right instead, the neutral asserted that its ships were to be touched only on grounds the law recognised, and that the flag carried commerce for all nations without thereby making the neutral a party to the war. The reply was therefore a claim to be treated according to the law of the sea, not a denial of the law itself.

questions.explanation: The reply made a claim of right so that the visit and seizure complained of would not become the measure of neutral treatment. It asserted the law of the sea, not an exemption from it.
questions.hint: A claim of right, not an apology.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a disputed return had no constitutional answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the answer to a disputed return had to achieve
questions.stem: Bought a nucleus of three frames in the spring, and I explained in the logbook why a disputed return had to be answered by law and practice, and what that answer had to achieve.

answer.exemplar: When two claimants returned for the same office, the constitution offered no rule to apply, and something had to be supplied: the count had to be conducted, objections had to be heard and recorded, and a result had to be announced that both the country and the losers could accept. The method that answered the dispute therefore had two requirements at once. It had to be settled in advance, so that the result did not depend on the temper of the persons counting, and it had to be public, so that the losing claimant could not simply declare the whole proceeding corrupt. Statute and custom together produced a course of procedure that met both needs without any clause in the text to support it.

questions.explanation: The answer had to be settled in advance and public, so the result did not turn on the counting's temper and the loser could not dismiss the proceedings. Statute and custom met both needs.
questions.hint: Settled in advance, and done in public.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission on industrial organisation
questions.learningObjective: List the lines of evidence the industrial commission gathered
questions.stem: I had to cut the tangles out of the brood frame, and I listed in the logbook the lines of evidence the commission on industrial organisation gathered, and how it used them.

options.text: The corporate records of the great companies, read for control and connection
The testimony of employers, organisers and public men about the working of the trade
The published price lists of the trade, checked against what firms actually charged
A single year's balance sheets, taken as a complete account of the industry
options.misconception: Treats one year of accounts as a complete survey

questions.explanation: The commission read the corporate records for control and connection and took the testimony of employers and organisers, then compared what was declared with what was charged.
questions.hint: Records, testimony, declared against actual.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two readings of combining production with distribution
questions.learningObjective: Identify the reading of combination expressed by a trade journal

stimulus.body: I copied this from the trade journal: the combination of the maker with the seller has been carried out in many trades, and in each the price to the consumer has been lower and the output larger than it was before the combination was made.

questions.stem: Bees nested in the shed wall, and I set the trade journal into the logbook and identified the reading of combination it expressed.

options.text: The reading that treats combination as a source of lower prices and larger output
The reading that treats combination as a device for closing a market to smaller firms
options.misconception: Confuses the defence of combination with the complaint about it

options.text: The reading that treats combination as unlawful whatever its price effect may be
options.misconception: Turns the price finding into a rule of illegality

options.text: The reading that treats the pre-combination price as the fair one to be restored
options.misconception: Invents a demand to restore the old price

questions.explanation: The journal gives the efficiency reading: combination brought lower prices and larger output, which is the case the advocates made. It says nothing of market closure or illegality.
questions.hint: Lower prices, larger output, and nothing else.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The shorter-hours argument and what it assumed
questions.learningObjective: Summarise the shorter-hours argument, its promise, and its assumption
questions.stem: Smoke made them climb the frame at last, and I wrote the summary of the shorter-hours argument, its promise, and the assumption beneath it.

options.text: A shorter day for the worker at the same pay, resting on the claim that output would not fall
A shorter day enforced by statute upon employers who had already agreed to it
options.misconception: Makes the employer's agreement the foundation of the reform

options.text: A shorter day for the worker at a lower hourly rate, so that total pay stayed unchanged
options.misconception: Turns the promise into a pay cut

options.text: A shorter day for the worker, with the increase shared with the employer through lower prices
options.misconception: Invents a price-sharing arrangement

questions.explanation: The promise was a shorter day at the same pay, resting on the claim that output would not fall, which employers contested. Enforcement by statute and pay cuts played no part in it.
questions.hint: Same pay, same output, shorter day.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: From a price agreement to a single corporation
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a forfeiture clause as the means of holding a price

stimulus.body: I copied this from the agreement: the parties agree that the price of the article shall be the sum stated, and that any party who sells below it shall forfeit his share of the deliveries and be excluded from the association.

questions.stem: Two swarms in one week, and I read the agreement into the logbook and asked what the forfeiture clause shows about how the price was to be made to hold.

options.text: That the agreement bound the members only because it carried a penalty for breaking it
That the price was set by the state and the parties only agreed to collect it
options.misconception: Makes the price a state tariff

options.text: That the members were bound by honour and by no sanction of any kind
options.misconception: Treats a written penalty as a matter of honour

options.text: That the agreement did not bind anyone and was kept only for the appearance of unity
options.misconception: Makes the penalty clause a sham

questions.explanation: The forfeiture clause supplied the sanction that made the price hold among members, which is why an agreement without a penalty bound nobody. The state set no tariff.
questions.hint: The penalty is what makes it bind.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A neutral's reply about armed merchant shipping
questions.learningObjective: State what a neutral insisted about the goods carried in its ships
questions.stem: Drawn comb sold to a neighbour, and I wrote in the logbook what a neutral government insisted about the goods carried in its ships, and where the limit of the claim lay.

options.text: That neutral ships could trade with all parties, contraband being judged by the law of the sea
That neutral ships must carry nothing that either belligerent had declared contraband
options.misconception: Accepts the belligerent's contraband list as binding on neutrals

options.text: That neutral ships could carry only goods belonging to their own nation's merchants
options.misconception: Restricts neutral cargo to national ownership

options.text: That once war began every neutral ship was subject to seizure without any ground
options.misconception: Makes all neutral shipping seizable at will

questions.explanation: A neutral insisted on trading with all parties, and the contraband question was settled by the law of the sea rather than by the belligerent's list. It neither surrendered the trade nor accepted seizure without ground.
questions.hint: All parties, with contraband judged by law.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two readings of the argument for entering the war
questions.learningObjective: Compare how the two readings could both be sincere
questions.stem: The extractor needed another drum, and I explained in the logbook why the two readings of the case for war could both be sincere, and where they were bound to clash.

answer.exemplar: The two readings were sincere because they were answering different questions that a country genuinely has to answer at once. One asked what the country would be willing to accept in the world and what it would say when other states were overrun, and it found the answer of right and of the protection of the weak. The other asked what the country would have to face if the war settled in favour of an industrial power it did not rival in strength, and it found the answer of trade, credit, and security. They were bound to clash over the means, because the moral reading expected the war to change the terms on which states were treated, while the security reading expected it to change the balance of power, and a government could pursue only one of them wholeheartedly at a time.

questions.explanation: Each reading answered a real question the country had to face, so both could be held sincerely, and they clashed over the means because one expected a change in law and the other in the balance of power.
questions.hint: Different questions, and different results.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a disputed return had no constitutional answer
questions.learningObjective: List the problems a disputed return raises and the shape of the answer
questions.stem: Uncapping knife slipped on the wet comb, and I listed in the logbook the problems a disputed return raises for the country, and the shape of the answer.

options.text: Two claimants claiming the same office, with the count of votes ungoverned by any text
A method of counting that had to be settled in advance and conducted in public
A rule that gave one of the two claimants the office by default
options.misconception: Invents a default rule favouring one claimant

options.text: An expectation that the loser would accept the result without any further contest
options.misconception: Assumes the loser must always accept

questions.explanation: A disputed return pits two claimants on the same office with a count the text does not govern, and the answer had to be a method settled in advance and conducted in public. No default rule favoured a claimant.
questions.hint: Two claimants, one office, no text.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission on industrial organisation
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a recommendation as evidence of a gap in the law

stimulus.body: I copied this from the report's closing paragraph: the commission recommends that the law be amended so that the occupation of boards of directors in competing companies shall be disclosed to the shareholders concerned, and that such occupation shall be made unlawful where it works to prevent competition.

questions.stem: Last nectar of the season drew the last bees, and I read the report's recommendation into the logbook and asked what it shows about the law the commission thought necessary.

options.text: That the existing law did not reach the overlap of directorships that concerned it
That the law needed extending to a practice the commission had found hard to control
options.misconception: Turns a gap in the law into a difficulty of control

options.text: That the problem was the size of the companies rather than the way they were governed
options.misconception: Redirects the finding from overlap to scale

options.text: That the remedy lay in lowering the duties paid to the directors of the great companies
options.misconception: Invents a remedy about director pay

questions.explanation: The recommendation to disclose and forbid certain overlapping directorships shows the commission thought the existing law did not reach the practice it had found. It did not treat size or pay as the problem.
questions.hint: The old law did not reach this practice.
